title: Why the Moon seems to follow your car
description: When you ride in a car at night, the trees whoosh past, the houses whoosh past — but the Moon stays right there, following you all the way home. Why?
author: SparkKindly · AI-assisted

body.heading: Near things rush, far things stay
paragraphs: Things close to the car — trees, fences, lamp posts — zoom past your window very fast. Things far away move past much more slowly. A mountain far away hardly seems to move at all.

The Moon is farther away than anything else you can see. It is so far that as your car drives along, the Moon looks like it is in exactly the same place — so it feels as if it is travelling with you, following your car home.

body.heading: Try the finger trick
paragraphs: Hold one finger up close to your nose and look at it. Now move your head a tiny bit. Your finger seems to jump! Now hold your finger far away, at arm's length, and move your head again. It jumps much less.
That is the Moon's secret. Faraway things hardly jump at all. The Moon is not really following you — it is just too far away to zoom past.

takeaway: The Moon only seems to follow your car because it is so very far away — near things zoom past, but faraway things stay in the same place.
ageGuidance: Ages 6-8: read aloud with a grown-up; best read before or after an evening car ride.
materials: This is a reading item — no materials needed
supervision: Read together with a grown-up; only look for the Moon from a parked car or as a passenger, never as the driver.
safetyNotes: Never lean out of a car window to look at the Moon.
Passengers only: the driver always watches the road.
screenFreeExtension: On your next evening walk, watch the Moon from two different streets and talk about how it stayed in the same part of the sky.
